opus-5.5.text:
Well, the fundamental challenge is that any watermark has to live in the text itself, in the choice of words, and the person trying to remove it has full control over that text once they have it. So the question becomes: how much do they have to change before the signal disappears?

The scheme I worked on at OpenAI is pretty simple at its core. Normally a language model samples each next token at random from some probability distribution. What we do instead is replace that randomness with a pseudorandom function keyed by a secret, so the choices are secretly biased in a way that nobody without the key can detect. Crucially, it's designed so the output distribution looks indistinguishable from normal: you don't degrade the quality of the text. But if you have the key, you can compute a score over the tokens, and with a few hundred tokens you get very high statistical confidence about whether the text came from GPT.

That's robust against a lot of things. If someone inserts or deletes a few words here and there, or rearranges some sentences, the signal mostly survives, because it's spread across the whole passage. The trouble is more systematic attacks. The obvious one is paraphrasing: run the output through a different language model that isn't watermarked and ask it to reword everything. Or there's the trick I like to describe, where you ask GPT to write the essay in Pig Latin, or to insert the word "banana" after every word, and then you strip those out yourself. Now the tokens the model actually chose aren't the tokens in the final text, and the watermark is gone.

So I've never claimed this is an unbreakable scheme. It's more like raising the cost of evasion. A lot of the people we're worried about, say a student who just pastes in an essay, or someone generating spam at scale, might not bother with those countermeasures. But a determined adversary can defeat it, and I think it's important to be honest about that.

There are deeper ideas floating around, like trying to watermark at the level of meaning rather than surface tokens, or combining watermarking with having the provider keep a database of what it generated and do some kind of semantic similarity search. Those help against paraphrasing, but they have their own problems with privacy and false positives. And then there's the policy problem, which is honestly harder than the technical one: a watermark only helps if the major providers actually deploy it, and as open-source models get better, people can always just use a model that doesn't watermark at all. So the hard part isn't only the cryptography; it's getting coordination among everyone building these systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, so the basic idea of the watermarking scheme that I worked on at OpenAI is pretty simple. Every time GPT generates a token, it's sampling from a probability distribution over what the next word or word-fragment should be. And what we do is we use a secret key, a cryptographic pseudorandom function, to bias that sampling—slightly—in a way that's statistically undetectable to anyone who doesn't have the key, but that someone who does have the key can later detect by looking at a few hundred tokens of text and seeing that there's a correlation that shouldn't be there by chance.

Now, the nice thing is that this doesn't degrade the quality of the output at all, in a precise sense, because on average over the key you're still sampling from exactly the same distribution. And it's pretty robust to simple things like deleting or inserting a few words, because the signal is spread out across the whole text—if you change ten percent of the tokens, you've only lost about ten percent of your signal.

But the main challenge, the one that I think is genuinely hard, is what you might call the paraphrase attack. If someone takes the watermarked text and then runs it through a different language model—or even just rewrites it themselves in their own words—then they're resampling essentially every token, and the watermark is gone. And there's really no way, at the level of the tokens, to prevent that. You could imagine trying to watermark at a deeper semantic level, embedding the signal in the choice of ideas or the structure of the argument rather than in the specific words, but then you're trading off against the quality of the output in a much more serious way, and even then I'm not sure it would survive a determined adversary.

So I tend to think of this honestly. Watermarking is not going to stop a sophisticated attacker who really wants to launder GPT output. What it does do is raise the cost. The student who wants to turn in an essay in ten minutes before the deadline, the content farm that wants to spit out ten thousand articles—those are the cases where you're not going to bother with a paraphrasing step, and that's actually a huge fraction of the use cases people are worried about. So I'd say the challenge is less "make it unbreakable," which I think is impossible, and more "make it a reasonable deterrent for the low-effort cases while being honest about what it can't do."

r002.rationale: The response identifies the challenge of embedding a watermark in deeper semantic features, such as ideas or argument structure, so it could survive paraphrasing.

astra-6.text:
Well, the main challenge is that text is very easy to transform while preserving its meaning. You can imagine a watermark that introduces a subtle statistical pattern into the model’s choice of words—something that a detector with the right key can recognize, but that a reader wouldn’t notice. The question is how much of that pattern survives when someone edits the text or asks another model to paraphrase it.

You’d like the watermark to survive ordinary changes, and you’d like removing it to require some real effort or loss of quality. But if someone rewrites the whole thing, there may simply be no signal left to detect. So the hard part is understanding what robustness we can actually achieve, under what kinds of attacks, without making the generated text worse or falsely flagging human writing.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the central difficulty is that text is very easy to transform while preserving its meaning. You can build a watermark by subtly biasing which words the model chooses, so that someone who knows the secret key can detect a statistical pattern. But then someone can take that output and paraphrase it, or run it through another model, and potentially wash out the pattern.

So the challenge is to make removing the watermark require a substantial change to the text, or a substantial amount of effort, while keeping the watermark imperceptible and preserving the quality of the output. And there are limits: if someone extracts the ideas and rewrites everything from scratch, you can’t reasonably expect a statistical watermark in the original wording to survive. The question is how much robustness we can get against practical attacks, rather than against every conceivable transformation.
